newsitem.title: POLAND: Michael Jackson eyes palace, theme park in Poland.
newsitem.headline: Michael Jackson eyes palace, theme park in Poland.

text.p: Singer Michael Jackson on Tuesday flew into Poland, where he feels loved, to consider building a major "EuroJackson" leisure park in Warsaw and restoring a vast 300-room palace to live in sometimes.

After an airport welcome by Warsaw's mayor and hundreds of shrieking schoolchildren, the King of Pop boarded a helicopter to fly over potential Warsaw sites for a possible theme park which officials said would cover more than 80 hectares.
Mayor Marcin Swiecicki told reporters that Jackson fell for Poland in September when he performed in Warsaw during his HIStory tour and met President Aleksander Kwasniewski.

"He said he was very moved by the reception he got in Warsaw last year," said Swiecicki, who visited Jackson in a Paris Disneyland hotel room earlier this month with a city delegation and has sent him proposals for investments.
"It is a good beginning. We will see what happens," the mayor said, adding Warsaw was hungry for leisure facilities.

Jackson, trailing a whiff of potential Saudi investment, has considered sites in Italy and other countries and Warsaw authorities were doing their best to lure him -- laying on a special welcome and experts to escort him.
Swiecicki said President Kwasniewski would see him again on Wednesday, when more details of possible projects may emerge.

Jackson last year signed a deal with Prince al-Waleed bin Talal bin Abdulaziz al-Saud, billionaire nephew of King Fahd of Saudi Arabia, to work together in joint ventures including concerts, films, television, theme parks and hotels.
Waleed once remarked: "I've got a rule of thumb: anything that's worth $4 billion and costs $1 billion -- buy it."

According to businessman Jacques Tourel, owner of Warsaw's biggest toyshop who is helping Jackson's search, the singer is also interested in buying and restoring a historic but run-down palace overlooking the Odra river near Wroclaw in western Poland.

"If he likes the palace, he may make his home base in Europe here in Poland," Tourel said, adding that the palace Jackson had in mind boasted 300 rooms, halls and other buildings on 50 hectares of land.

He said it could rival Elvis Presley's former U.S. home Graceland as a tourist attraction, adding: "Michael is now ten times bigger than Elvis. Can you imagine how many people may now come to visit his home and museum?".
He said the proposed "EuroJackson" theme park would have a special flavour imparted by the star to draw his fans.

Jackson himself did not speak publicly after climbing from a private jet, clad in a black jacket crossed with gold braid, a black hat and dark glasses, to watch a childrens' dance troupe perform a traditional mazurka in historic court outfits.

The head of Warsaw Central District's development, Jerzy Guz, accompanying Jackson, said the Poles were hoping for firmer indications of Jackson's plans during the trip but so far he had mainly spoken warmly of his liking for the country.
"At present we are talking about emotions rather than business," Guz said at Warsaw's military airport.
City officials declined to reveal the locations Jackson was examining or the size of any potential investment.
